summary:
SURE provides NASA logistics planners with route readiness scores before and after tropical cyclone, enabling launch vehicle cargo to pre-positioned via passable route.

Hurricane Katrina (2005) shut down Stennis Space Center and Michoud Assembly Facility for about a month, with an initial NASA loss estimates of US$1.1 billion. Damaged roads and flooding impeded access and made supply corridors hard to assess. Risk is also escalating, as NASA supported launches rose from 31 in 2021 to 109 in 2025. While infrastructure nears capacity limits in the 2028 - 2029.

NISAR & GUNW products identify flooded roads and landslide affected areas by detecting changes in decibels (dB) of backscatter and temporal coherence, and radar can penetrate cloud cover. METEO meteorological data forecast weather conditions over the following days. Each route receives a readiness score with data quality and data age indicators.

NISAR acquires data only every 12 days. Therefore, SURE provides a data age indicator and flags routes with temporal coherence below 0.5 for field verification. Planners can reposition supplies before the hurricane arrives and choose routes that remain passable afterward, reducing delay risk and cost exposure.
details:
SURE provides readiness route scores before and after a hurricane, with open, slowed, or blocked flags. As a result, planners can quickly switches to other mode s through sea, land, or air. Katrina is a sample case nearly complete shuttle external tanks sat at Michoud. Impact from flooded roads and washed out bridges made them hard to reach. Therefore the next shuttle flight slipped to May 2006. A Preliminary estimate put damage and related costs at up to US$1.1 billion. Risk is also escalating, as NASA supported launches rose from 31 in 2021 to 109 in 2025, while infrastructure nears capacity limits in 2028 - 2029. Not only that, critical supplier are limited like carbon fiber has only three suppliers.

SURE uses NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) and GUNW (Geocoded UNWrapped interferogram) products to measure backscatter change in decibels (dB) and temporal coherence, which determine whether water exists at the route coordinates and whether a landslide has occurred. This data comes from NASA services such as GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services), EONET (Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker), and POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources). The procedure is as follows:

- Find 5 distinct routes using a penalty method (+4% cost per reused segment), accepting those at most 1.25× the shortest route and sharing at most 80% of roads with others.

- Take the worst color between K1 (backscatter change) and K2 (if available).

- Add up the extra travel time caused by slower yellow and red segments.

- Apply a rain speed reduction only to wet-prone segments, using the highest rain level among 3 route points on the selected date.

- Display the red segment count only, since red segments already slow the route through the 0.47 factor.

- Score each route by travel time in minutes (base time + radar penalty + rain penalty) and mark the fastest with star, following Wardrop's first principle.

- Sum each segment's travel time, calculated from base speed adjusted by color and rain factors.

- Take the worst color among all segments, so a single red segment makes the whole route red.

To provide weather forecasts, we use Open-Meteo to predict cyclones up to 8 days ahead (and up to 5 years ahead using machine learning), and Open-Meteo Marine to calculate wind direction. Furthermore, we use mapping technologies such as OSM, Overpass, OSRM, and Nominatim, together with React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and a custom canvas engine, so users can access our platform easily. For the logic behind our proposed solution, SURE uses Gemini, the GitHub Contents API, a localStorage fallback, GitHub Pages, and GitHub Actions. SURE combines cloud penetrating radar with weather forecasts to fill the 12-day gap between satellite passes, and it runs entirely in the browser.

Our team considered several limitations in the current prototype. The thresholds come from C-band studies, so they need recalibration for NISAR's L-band data. The speeds and penalty values are team assumptions, and the long-distance truck speed of 72 kmph has not been verified. In addition, the weather shown in the mockup is simulated and clearly labeled as such.

SURE helps planners position supplies before a hurricane arrives and gives them earlier, clearer visibility of which routes or transport modes are open, so they can reroute before a barge or truck is committed. This lets them choose routes that stay passable. The intended impact is to reduce delay and cost exposure, which means less schedule slip from access problems.

Note: Super Intelligence helped us create part of the project details content.

ATTACHEMENT

  1. Bader et al. (2010): Supports the alternative-route method. The penalty factor of 0.4 (0.3 with multi-increase) was tuned by experiment on 100 random origin-destination pairs. It is not a theoretical value, so it should be sensitivity-tested for SURE.
  2. Correa et al. (2004): Justifies using travel time as the route score. Under Wardrop's first principle, travelers choose routes by travel time, so the fastest route is the best one.
  3. Dinner (2026): Source for NASA-supported launches rising from 31 (2020) to 109 (2025) on the Florida Space Coast. It also shows the renewal gap: the goal is every 66 years, but the current rate is over 260 years.
  4. NASA OIG, audit (n.d.): Shows that weather disruption is real. Artemis I slipped by over a month because of Hurricane Ian, plus a few days for Hurricane Nicole, in 2022. It also shows that centers don't consistently use their risk assessments.
  5. NASA OIG, news release (2026): Shows launches at Kennedy and Wallops rose 252% and 467%. Both sites are expected to near capacity in 2028-2029. Real-term construction and maintenance budgets fell 11-47% over 5 years.
  6. PwC & AIA (2026): Shows the supply side is fragile. Carbon-fiber composites have only three major US aerospace-grade suppliers. Switchgear lead times reach up to 27 months. Capacity utilization hit 74% in Dec 2025.
  7. ULA (2022): A real sea-leg benchmark. RocketShip left Decatur on 14 Feb, arrived at Port Canaveral on 23 Feb, and finished offloading on 24 Feb. The "about one day to unload" claim is your inference from these dates, so word it that way.
  8. WHO (2017): Supports the road speed assumptions, since speed management matters for safety and urban limits are about 50 km/h. Check the "1 in 3 deaths" and "47 countries" figures on the full page before citing them.
